subject: knightSnail
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: knight jousting on a snail.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I need to plan a single TypeScript module carefully, keeping risk low by sticking to well-understood APIs. For the visual style, rather than the obvious heraldic/medieval tapestry approach for knights, I'm leaning toward something more unexpected like stained-glass or leaded-glass with a glowing translucent quality.

Actually I'm now drawn to Delftware porcelain — a cobalt blue-and-white ceramic figurine aesthetic with tiny gold lustre accents, floral brushwork decals on the shell, blue spiral swirls painted along the shell's curve, and the knight rendered in tin-glazed white armor with blue linework. I'll scale the model realistically: the snail's body around 1.6m long with a 0.9m shell, the knight mounted near the front of the body ahead of the shell.

I'm now working out the pose and proportions: the knight sits saddled on the snail's foot behind its head, shell trailing behind, lance couched forward over the eye stalks and shield on the left arm. I'm settling on a warhorse-scaled snail — body around 3m long, shell 1.5m diameter — with the knight seated around 0.7m up, and I'm defining the coordinate layout for the sweeping foot shape from tail to raised, horse-like neck, plus the head with its eye stalks.

Now I'm designing the skeleton rig: a spine chain running along the snail's body, a neck and head with jaw and eye-stalk joints, a shell joint, and a separate knight skeleton with hips, spine, arms and legs attached as a child of the snail body. I'm working out how to make sure there's a single explicit root joint ("hips") that all the chains parent to correctly.

I'm plotting coordinates along the snail's centerline from tail to head to give it a natural swan-neck curve rising toward a head positioned around 1.0m high, with the mouth slightly forward, and sizing the shell and foot proportionally so the knight sitting on the back looks roughly human-scale when seated.

For the shell itself, I'm sweeping a tube along a spiraling path that grows outward to one side, tapering the tube radius geometrically from a wide aperture down to a narrow tip to mimic a real snail shell's coiling shape.

Generating spiral tube points...

With 10 sides and roughly 108 rings across three turns, I'll have plenty of triangles for a smooth tube with a rounded cap at the aperture end. I'm now worried about self-intersection between adjacent whorls, since with a decay ratio of about 0.45 per turn the radial gap shrinks to 0.55R while the tube diameter is 0.84R — meaning the tube is wider than the gap and whorls will overlap.

That overlap is actually realistic though, since real snail shells have fused, overlapping whorls, and visually intersecting tube geometry renders fine for a puppet model. For coloring, I'm thinking of a Delft-style palette: white ground with cobalt blue spiral stripe bands following the whorl direction, controlled by the angle-around-tube coordinate, possibly adding a dot pattern or decal motif on the outer face.

For orientation, the shell's spiral should lie roughly in the YZ-plane with the axis pointing toward +X, giving a conical shape as the pitch winds inward; I need to figure out where the aperture connects to the body versus where the apex points, matching how a real snail shell attaches at its underside-front.

Actually a planispiral disc shape makes more sense for a cartoon snail shell—symmetric about x=0 so the spiral reads from both sides, with the outer whorl tube radius scaled to roughly 0.29 given R0=0.7, giving the shell some thickness along x.

Now I'm working out shell placement on the knight's body: with the shell center around (0, 1.05, -0.85) and R0=0.7, the outer whorl's lowest point sinks down into the body mesh there, so I need the shell to rest properly above the torso rather than clipping through it.

Shell tail now extends to -1.85 with rear extent -1.88, which fits well behind the body. Now I'm working out the spiral parameterization for the shell—starting angle near the front-bottom aperture around -50°, and figuring out which rotational direction the whorl should wind in to match a natural shell look.

I'll just pick a convention: tracing from the aperture inward, φ increases, sweeping front → top → back → bottom, so the tube spirals upward and backward from its opening.

Working out the decay math: with total 2.6 turns and radius shrinking from 0.62 to 0.1, each successive whorl shrinks by about half, with tube radius around 0.4R per whorl so neighboring whorls overlap slightly for a tight, realistic packing.

I'll make the tube cross-section slightly elliptical, wider along the binormal direction than the normal, and build a radius function that interpolates cross-section dimensions from a precomputed arc-length table rather than a single scalar.

For the shell's paint, I'm attaching it to the shell bone and planning stripe bands based on angle around the tube — need to figure out which angular positions correspond to visible outer faces versus the dorsal/ventral orientation given the spiral lies in the YZ plane, which is a bit disorienting to reason about.

Working through the derivative confirms the front-most point sits at φ=0, with z increasing as φ moves from -50° toward zero—so the aperture starts lower-front and the tube sweeps forward-up to that extreme before curving over.

Now I'm figuring out the rotational clock convention for the tube's cross-section: 0° marks the inner side facing toward the spiral's center, 180° the outer side, and 90°/270° mark the flank sides perpendicular to that, using parallel transport so the normal stays consistent along the tangent. This means any stripe or bulge I want on the flanks should be painted at the 90° and 270° positions.

For the shell's decoration, I'm planning a Delft-style pattern: a spiral pinstripe centered on each visible flat face, plus cross-ribs simulating growth lines that get denser as the radius shrinks toward the apex, an outlined edge along the outer 180° band, and a blue wash that intensifies near the apex until it's nearly solid blue. I'm checking that this paint logic works correctly when applied along the sweep's parametric position, then shifting to painting the snail's body itself with a white base and blue countershading pattern.

For the body, I'm layering a scaled texture with blue outlines to mimic skin and cobbled Delft hatching, using a countershade function so the back is patterned white/blue while the belly fades to pale blue. I'm settling on a cohesive Delft color palette — cream-white glaze, cobalt and deep blue, pale and mid blues, cream shadow, and a sparing gold lustre accent for the tip or crown — committing to a blue-and-white scheme with just a touch of gold.

Since I can't directly tweak material roughness through the normal API, I'm planning to traverse the mesh after reading the baked root and manually lower roughness on any MeshStandardMaterial for a glossier glaze look, since materials are shared by color and this should be harmless. Now I'm starting to think through the snail's head details — eye stalks with rounded eye bulbs, possibly using a decal for the eyes.

I'm also designing a heraldic caparison, the draped cloth covering the knight's snail mount, as a slightly larger loft over the body sweep with a checked diamond lozenge pattern painted using a coordinate-based tiling function.

I need the path's y-coordinates to track with the radius so the sole stays flush at the bottom, allowing a tiny 1% sink rather than a full offset shift.

Mapping out the body profile from tail to neck now, defining positions and radii at each station along the snail's curve.

I'm sizing the snail to about 4 meters, a proper steed for the knight, and working out how he sits astride the back near the neck's rise. The tricky part is positioning his legs so they drape naturally along the wide flanks without clipping into the body, so I'm thinking through hip placement and thigh angle to keep him seated believably.

Placing the knee outward at x≈±0.55-0.6 keeps it clear of the body, and I'm checking the leg segment lengths work out for thigh and shin proportions. I'll define the leg as a simple hip-knee-ankle chain with explicit joint positions rather than solving inverse kinematics.

Now I'm thinking through overall scale: the knight sits around 1.35m tall with the seat at y=0.62 and head near the top, while the snail itself should be rendered much larger than a normal human-scale rider, giving a heroic, oversized composition.

Adjusting the shell center and extending the tail tip slightly further out. For the knight's pose, I'm working out the couched lance position in the right hand, angled diagonally forward across the mount's neck toward the left, from grip point near the saddle to a tip extending well in front, roughly 2.8 meters long plus the butt extension behind.

Checking whether the lance's path at the point it crosses the snail's neck collides with the head geometry—it looks like it would clip through the head at that height, so I need to either raise the lance's trajectory or lower the snail's neck/head profile to clear it.

I'm working out the geometry so the lance threads neatly between the eye stalks at x≈0, calculating the grip and tip positions and slope needed to keep it clear of the head and stalk widths.

Checking the lance length against historical proportions, it ends up near 4.3 meters, which is a bit long but plausible. Now I'm placing the right arm joints so the hand height and couched position under the armpit make sense relative to the shoulder.

Reconsidering the lance's angle, I decide a slight upward tilt from grip to tip works better—keeping it clear of the figure's head and giving it a raised, ceremonial charge look.

Working out positions along the lance: hand grip is placed 20% along from butt to tip, which lands around (-0.37, 1.09, 0.72), then I figure the shoulder-to-hand IK with the elbow bending down and outward for a natural arm pose.

At the head end of the lance (around z=2.0), I compute the lance crosses near the midline while positioning the eye stalks slightly out to either side so they flank it without colliding, tapering the lance's radius from thin near the tip to thicker at the grip.

Checking the shield on the left arm, I'm placing it near the hand position, angled outward about 40° so its front face is visible, sized roughly 0.5 wide by 0.7 tall, and confirming it sits far enough from the lance's x-position (around -0.34) to avoid overlap.

I'm also setting up the shield's heraldic decal, computing its thickness axis via a cross product so the extrusion faces outward correctly to match the shield's facing direction.

I'll overlay the SVG shield face (rim, field, snail emblem, border) on the extruded shape, then move to building the knight's body: armored pieces like the cuirass, pauldrons, gorget, helmet with visor slit and plume, limb sweeps with gauntlets, poleyns, sabatons, and a heraldic tabard with the snail motif over a fauld skirt.

For pose, I'll go with a jousting stance (arms holding lance and shield) rather than a neutral rest pose, since that fits the subject better. For the great helm, I'm shaping it as a lathed cylinder with a flat top profile, adding a visor slit decal, breathing holes, and an extruded crest plume in blue and white gradient at the back.

The face stays hidden behind the closed helm, though I'll give a hint of dark eye slits, and I'm considering a hinged visor joint analogous to a creature's jaw mechanism. The knight will face forward along +Z with the torso kept straight. Now I'm moving into the joint skeleton setup, naming the root joint and sketching out a spine chain from tail to neck with defined positions for each segment.

Rethinking the hierarchy, I prefer a mid-body "core" joint with two separate chains branching out -- one toward the head, one toward the tail -- rather than a single tail-to-head chain, since that avoids having tail movement drag the entire body. This mirrors an example approach from the documentation, so I'll structure the knight's hips as a child of this central core joint instead of a mid-chain joint.

Splitting the body path into three slices—tail, spine, neck—and deriving each chain's joint count from the number of knots along that slice, with the neck chain parented to the spine's final joint.

I'm checking that `closestT` works correctly on arc-length parametrized slices, then thinking through how to build the body radius function by mapping each station's position to a `t` value along the full body path and interpolating radii between them.

The radius functions take the source t along the body sweep, using the same bone chain of tail/core/spine/neck for both body and caparison layers. For the caparison, I'm sweeping the same path again but wider, with flat cloth-hem caps and a trim color, though I need to check whether the flat ends will show awkwardly near the snail's sole.

I work out that shifting the caparison section by about 0.025-0.03 along the normal axis keeps its bottom edge flush at y=0 while letting the top billow outward like draped cloth, so the flat sole issue is a non-problem.

I plan to finish the hem with small blue trim loops at both ends and add triangular pennant teeth hanging along the edge for a decorative, scalloped finish.

Actually those downward spikes at the lower half would end up tucked inside the body tube and hidden from view, so I should drop that idea entirely. Simpler to just do the trim loop band and a diamond paint pattern, skip the dagged edges and tassels, and move on to something else instead.

Now I'm planning a heraldic emblem decal for the caparison's flanks—a blue sun or snail-shell symbol facing both +X and −X sides. I need to budget carefully, targeting 180-340 parts and roughly 700+ lines of code with reusable helpers, so I'm sketching out the texture list: an eye texture for stalk eyes with iris, pupil, and highlight mapped via decal onto the eye bulb sphere, followed by a shield-face texture next.

I'm also designing a tabard chest emblem with a snail-shell rose motif, a Delft-inspired tulip bouquet decal for the caparison flank (playing on the classic Delft blue tile aesthetic), and a visor/helm decal with an eye-slit and cross-breath pattern. For the lance I'm considering a pennon texture with Delft-style stripes rendered as a double-sided card attached near the lance tip.

For the helmet plume I'm thinking of using small feather-textured cards fanned along the crest line, collecting placement frames by walking along the crest path and pushing each sampled position into an array to drive the card instances.

For the plume orientation I want frames pointing backward along the arc from the helmet top, and rigging all the cards to the head bone so they move together as a single unit. I'm also considering whether painted textures still need to be tallied separately, and ruling out any ground tiles since there's no ground element called for in the scene.

Switching gears, I'm now sketching the snail-knight details: no base needed, keep the visor as the eye texture, skip the lance emblem, and leave glow effects off since gold accents work fine as flat color. For the stalks, I'm planning tentacle chains with tapered radius and eye bulbs at the tips, shorter feeler chains below, and a loft-built head with separate upper lip and lower jaw pieces rigged to the jaw joint for that cute grin -- now working out the neck joint placement to anchor it all.

I'm laying out the body profile as a series of positioned, radius-tapered stations from tail to neck, with the foot lifting slightly near the front before the neck rises up to the head base joint, then placing an ellipsoid head just ahead of that joint to cap off the shape.

I'm setting up the bone chain (tail, core, spine, neck) and using a nearest-joint lookup to attach the hip joint to the spine for the knight's pose, then starting on the saddle geometry with a pommel and cantle shape to seat the rider.

Now I'm laying out the knight's own skeleton rig, placing pelvis, torso, and chest joints along a spine chain for the seated figure.

I need unique joint names across both rigs — head, neck, jaw for recognizable rigging, but since the knight is humanoid and the snail is the mount, I'll give the knight those standard names and find alternatives for the snail's head joint to avoid collisions.

I'm setting up the full naming scheme: knight gets hips, spine chain, neck, head, visor; snail gets a root "core" plus snailHead and snailJaw. For joint creation, each non-root joint needs an explicit parent, and I'm defining the arm chain as a three-point path (shoulder, elbow, wrist) with sides determined by x-sign convention, R being negative x.

For hands I'm keeping things simple—blocky gauntlet fists with a thumb but skipping a full finger chain to limit joint count, since the right hand grips the lance anyway. For legs I'm using the same three-point path approach as the arms: hip, knee, ankle per side, naming them hipL/kneeL/ankleL with the ankle as the chain tip.

I'll add a sabaton foot piece attached to the ankle bone, and render the limb chains as smooth sweeps rather than rigid segments. For armor detailing I'm layering on couters, poleyns, and rerebrace rings at the joints, then building the torso as a loft along the spine bones with waist, chest, and shoulder stations sized to taper appropriately, finished with a blue-and-white Delft-style paint pattern on the cuirass.

Writing paint functions...

Using scales for the snail — white with blue edges, echoing the classic Delft tile scale motif with some mottled drift. For the armor I'm thinking cobalt wash with white rivets, using a panelled pattern with defined rivet size and dark seam color.

Thinking about gold-toned rivets for the clockwork armor to complement the cobalt — but I'm wary of importing a kit module since the SDK path conventions are uncertain and could fail. Safer to write my own simple paint helpers instead of relying on the clockwork kit.

I need to watch for strict TypeScript settings like noUnusedParameters and noUnusedLocals, so I'll keep imports and variables all actually used, and add explicit types where needed. Starting the Delftware-style figurine build now, importing THREE and the builder utilities...

Setting up color palette and vector helpers...

Writing more paint functions...

Writing shell paint function...

Now I'm working out the angular math for where the pinstripes should fall around the shell's flanks, figuring out which degree ranges correspond to the sides versus the inner/outer curve.

Still writing shell banding logic...

That said, I'm not fully confident the dorsal clock mapping is exact, but any consistent decorative pattern should still read as plausible shell striping even if bands land slightly off from a "real" reference.

I'll use the flank-angle formula and just arc fraction for position along the shell. For style, I'm deciding against extra tile decals or a lustre rim—keeping the shell joint simple at point C.

Writing shell point generator function...

Actually, thinking about the overall shape: a pure planispiral feels too flat, so I want to add a slight conical pitch along one axis to give it a more recognizable snail-shell silhouette rather than a nautilus-like flat coil.

I'm building the tube radius function using an arc-length lookup table for consistent sweeping, then setting up the sweep call with tapered ends, a rounded cap at the start, and a pointed cone cap at the end, using 10-sided rings for the cross-section.

Thinking about shading next: using flat (non-smooth) shading on the shell for a faceted porcelain look rather than smooth circular shading. I'm also planning a thin gold line swept along the outer ridge of the shell surface to add a lustrous accent detail.

For the snail's head, I'm sketching an ellipsoid-based sphere geometry for the head, scaled and positioned to form the cranium and muzzle, separate from the lower jaw joint, with a wide "smiling" mouth design and a head joint positioned above and forward of the body.

I'll skip teeth and give the jaw a slight open pose with a pale blue interior for a simple grin effect. For positioning the eye stalks, I'm defining them consistently using forward/up/left-right words relative to the head's local coordinate frame, branching symmetrically from a base point near the top of the head.

Now I'm plotting a curved path for each stalk using Catmull-Rom points that sweep up and outward before reaching the tip, then chaining tentacle joints along that path with a tapering sweep radius.

I'm adding an eye bulb sphere at the stalk tip with low-poly flat shading, then projecting a round blue eye decal onto its front surface, positioning and orienting it so it faces slightly forward and outward—mirrored the same way for both sides.

For the smaller feeler tentacles I'll give them simple nub spheres without eyes, and for the cheeks I'm applying a small decorative swirl decal to each side of the head to mimic a painted blue blush mark.

Skipping a distinct nose feature, I'm thinking about adding a thin blue wave-line sweep along the flanks for extra decoration, using the body sweep path at a given angle so the tube follows the surface and inherits its bone weights automatically.

Now I'm shifting to the knight's torso placement, working out the pelvis, seat, and body top coordinates relative to the cushion height.

Working out the shell top height so the plume clears it, giving a total figure height near 2.25. Now I'm repositioning the lance so it passes between the snail's head stalks, adjusting hand position below the shoulder and recomputing the butt coordinates to fit the slope.

I'm checking the stalk geometry stays clear of the lance path, and confirming the lance doesn't intersect the shield or snail head given their positions in z and y.

Now shaping the lance itself: tapering its radius from butt to tip, painting blue-and-white barber-pole stripes along its length, adding a bell-shaped vamplate guard near the grip, and finishing with a steel-blue coronel spike tip ringed in gold before starting on the pennon flag.

Working out the pennon's orientation, with the flag streaming backward from the tip along the lance's axis, using a perpendicular up-vector to define the extrusion plane correctly.

For the pennant coloring, I'm computing diagonal cobalt/white stripe bands using a floor function on the surface coordinates, plus a gold fringe trim, keeping the flag flat rather than adding a wave bend. For the knight's body, I'm planning a cobalt cuirass with gold rivet dots and a white surcoat/tabard with a blue chest border, considering a simpler loft over the torso for the tabard panels.

Now I'm defining torso loft stations running from hips to neck base, specifying position, width, and height at each level (hips, waist, chest, shoulder, neck) to shape the cuirass and tabard, before moving on to building the spine bone chain.

I want the spine chain to catmull-interpolate through those station centers, producing named joints like spineK1 and spineK2, then adding separate neck and head joints parented up that chain with their own aim directions. For the torso loft itself I'm tying it to the spine chain as its bone path, then planning a slightly larger second loft for the surcoat/tabard layered over the base armor.

For the surcoat I'm thinking of painting the cuirass itself glaze white with a decal emblem on the chest, keeping the gorget, pauldrons, and belt in cobalt and gold so the blue plate shows through against the white cloth look. I'm also sketching a flared hip skirt as a lathed or extruded outline draping over the thighs for a seated rider, working out the point sequence so the profile doesn't self-intersect.

Writing shoulder armor geometry...

Still shaping the pauldron geometry...

Positioning the dome outline slightly above the shoulder, then shifting focus to the arm structure—figuring out whether to rig the shoulder as a rigid joint tied to the arm chain, and starting to define the arm sweep with a tapering radius profile.

Now I'm working out the arm sweep: a tapering radius from upper arm to forearm along the chain, ending at the wrist joint, with the hand built as a boxy cobalt gauntlet shape rather than individual fingers.

For the wrist joint, I'm mirroring that grip setup for the left hand holding a shield strap. I'm positioning the shield at roughly (0.62, 1.1, 0.9) with its face angled at 50 degrees, and now working out the shield's half-width dimensions to match.

Checking the shield's size and tilt to make sure its edges don't collide with the body or caparison—since it sits above the body's top at y 1.1, floating clear in the air, that should be fine geometrically.

Moving to the right arm, I'm verifying the shoulder-elbow and elbow-hand segment lengths come out roughly consistent (~0.3-0.34), which checks out.

Now I'm recomputing the leg hip-to-knee positions to see if the thigh geometry still clears the body at the given knee x-offset.

Checking the knee width against the body's half-width at that height, the thigh touches but doesn't overlap, and the thigh length comes out to about 0.53, which is fine. Tracing the shin from knee to ankle gives a length near 0.48, and the ankle position sits clear of the body flank, so the shin passes outside without intersecting. I'm now thinking about adding stirrups as iron loops hanging from the saddle.

Now I'm sketching the stirrup setup: a torus ring at the foot with a thin leather strap rod connecting it up to the saddle. For the foot, I'm planning a tapered capsule shape sweeping from ankle to toe to form a pointed sabaton boot, plus a heel box, keeping the foot's lowest point just above the floor so the knight appears to hang slightly rather than stand. For the helmet, I'm positioning a great helm on the head joint, sizing it a bit larger than the head itself to account for padding, with the rim sitting at the neck and the crown extending upward.

I'm lathing out the helm's profile from a dome-shaped outline along the central axis, then painting it cobalt with white decorative bands, like a Delft-style scroll pattern across the forehead. For the visor, I'm adding a horizontal slit decal with small cross-hole "breath" patterns, projected onto the front surface of the helm as a texture, and giving it two small glinting white eye dots inside the dark slit for a cute touch. Now I'm starting to think through a crest or plume ridge extruded along the top of the helm.

Now I'm shaping the crest as an arced fin along the top of the helm with gold-cobalt coloring, then adding seven feather-textured plume cards angled progressively from 30 to 80 degrees as they sweep backward, each card double-sided so the feather texture reads from both angles. After that I'm adding a cobalt gorget collar at the neck with a white ring trim, a snail-shell emblem decal on the chest tabard, and sketching out a cape membrane that drapes from the shoulders backward over the snail's shell, built as a swept surface between two trailing edge paths.

I'm working out how the cape hangs down behind the knight without clipping into the shell geometry, defining its two edges as curves running from each shoulder down toward trailing points, then adding border trim coloring along the cape's length and attaching it to the chest spine joint for proper bone weighting.

Skipping a crown decoration and reins for simplicity, I'm instead giving the snail a head harness — a cobalt band looping around the head plus a gold chanfron-style plate on the forehead, shaped like a kite between the eye stalks with a decorative tulip motif.

Now I'm sizing the snail's head ellipsoid and positioning it so the lance clears above, then building the jaw and mouth as a dark wedge beneath the head center.

I'm deciding to skip extra details like nostrils and tassels to keep the part count manageable, focusing instead on simpler elements like cheek swirl decals and a diamond-patterned caparison, and starting a rough tally of parts needed to hit the target count.

Tallying up: snail body, caparison trims and lines, shell, head and stalks, feelers and cheeks, harness and saddle, then the knight's torso, belt, skirt, arms with pauldron lames, legs with greaves and sabatons, helm, plume, cape, lance, shield, and stirrups—roughly 120 parts so far. I'm thinking about padding this out further with repeated details like rivets, shell studs, and gold stud rows along the caparison hem to push toward the 180+ target.

Considering small decorative flourishes too—tile-corner decals, shell rosette decals, maybe tulip motifs on the cape or caparison flank, since quality matters more than exact count. I'm also checking that the snail's body silhouette actually touches down at y=0, making sure the catmull-rom interpolation between stations doesn't undershoot and leave a gap at the base.

Writing helper types and vector math functions...

Writing blob helper function...

I'm also checking whether `Frame` should be imported, and whether the `scale` option on `part` can take a vector array rather than just a number, based on how the toon example uses it.

Now I'm defining the shell joint, positioning it near the back and choosing its parent -- likely the core joint, since the tail chain can also branch off that same parent.

Working out the spiral path parameters and tube radii for the shell geometry...

Checking for overlaps: the shell's forward extent clears the knight/cape, and while the shell's lowest point dips slightly into the body near that station, it's a minor intentional overlap for a merged look rather than a collision.

Verifying the spiral's starting angle places the aperture right at the body's top radius near z=-0.6, so the cap's opening naturally nestles into the body without a visible gap.

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy, starting with a core joint acting as the spine root, then defining the body's station points and radii in a lookup table.

Building the body curve from the stations and mapping each station's z-position to its parameter along that curve, so I can later look up radius by t and slice the path into neck, root, and other segments for different body sections.

I'm setting up chains for the spine, neck, and tail sections, each parented appropriately (tail and spine off the core, neck off the last spine joint), with specific joint counts for each. Then I'm defining the head joint anchored at the end of the neck chain, positioned at the tip of the body path.

Now I'm placing the head ellipsoid so it overlaps the body's rounded end to hide the seam, then adding a jaw joint and mouth pieces like the upper lip positioned relative to the head.

Defining head sub-parts: cranium, muzzle, mouth interior, lower jaw...

Skipping fangs and extra boxes, I'm keeping eyelids simple and letting the brow sit within the eye texture itself rather than modeling it separately. For the cheek, I'm placing a decal onto the cranium using a local offset and direction relative to the head frame.

Now I'm working out the harness: a loop traced around the cranium using a plane cut, swept into a closed cobalt band that inherits the surface's bone weights, then studded with gold balls spaced along its path. Next I'm thinking about a chanfron-style gold plate for the forehead gem.

Working out the stalk's curve, plotting a sequence of points that bend forward and outward as they rise from the base to the tip, checking the height math so the tip lands around 1.6-1.7m and clears the lance position around 1.4m.

The eye bulb sits at the top of the stalk, giving it a radius for the eye socket and deciding the eye's facing direction so it points slightly outward and forward, then I set up the stalk's sweep shape with a skin-colored tube that tapers from thicker at the base to thinner near the tip, and start plotting the base and next segment points for the lower feeler stalks.

Now I'm planning out the knight's arm structure: writing a helper function that builds an arm chain from shoulder to elbow to hand, tagging it with left/right naming based on sign, then sweeping a tapered tube shape along the chain for the arm's thickness.

Placing cuffs along the chain's tangent frame so rings orient naturally around the arm...

point so embed 0.5 centers it on the frame point, and embed 0 lets it extend outward from the point instead. For blended frames spanning two bones, part should handle smooth weighting automatically, so I don't need to worry about that case specially.

Legs will follow the same pattern, with the ankle as the tip joint. I'll write a small helper function for armor bands that takes a chain, parameter, radius, height, and color, then move on to defining the fist capsules using a lance point parameter.

Writing fist and shield geometry...

Finishing the tulip's leaves and bloom shapes, then listing the texture set I need: eye, cheek swirl, shield, tabard, flank emblem, visor, and feather — seven total. For the flank emblem decal, I'm placing mirrored copies on each side of the caparison sweep, and working out the orientation math so the artwork reads correctly from both viewing angles given the facing and up vectors.

For the visor decal, I'm sketching an SVG with a dark navy eye-slit, white eyes with blue pupils inside, a row of cross-dot breathing holes below, and a gold cross motif down the faceplate, keeping the cobalt-and-white Delft palette consistent with the helm.
